explanations.answer: To block anyone going in or out of Judah
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Baasha fortified Ramah "to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah." Imagine somebody parking a truck across the only road out of your neighborhood. Nobody's getting in, and nobody's getting out.

explanations.answer: To guard his own border against the Philistines
explanations.explanation: Close, because it does have to do with a border. But the text never mentions the Philistines here. Baasha was building at Ramah against Judah, to keep anyone from leaving or entering Asa's territory. So this wall was aimed at Asa's side, not at anybody else.

explanations.answer: To build a brand new capital for Israel
explanations.explanation: Nope, no new capital in this story, baker. The text says Baasha went up against Judah and fortified Ramah to stop anyone from leaving or entering Asa's territory. That's a roadblock, not a building project for a new home. Nobody throws a housewarming party at a roadblock.

explanations.answer: The treasuries of the temple and palace
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Asa withdrew the silver and gold "from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace." That means he reached into both places and took it out. I think that's a lot of silver and gold to hand over to somebody else.

explanations.answer: The ships that bring gold from Ophir
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but no ships show up in this passage. The text says Asa took the silver and gold out of the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace. It was already sitting in storage, and he pulled it out. No ships needed.

explanations.answer: The yearly tribute from the land of Moab
explanations.explanation: Moab doesn't come into this story at all, friend. Asa withdrew the silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace. So it came from his own storage, not from some payment arriving from another land.

You got it, baker. Asa sent the silver, the gold and his message to Ben-hadad king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus. Aram was the neighbor Asa was hoping would turn things around for him. That's a whole lot of treasure to put on a messenger's back.
Hiram king of Tyre isn't in this story, friend. The text says the silver and gold went to Ben-hadad king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus. So Asa's messenger was headed to Damascus, not to Tyre.
Shishak king of Egypt never shows up here, baker. The silver and gold went to Ben-hadad king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus. Asa's message had a very specific address, and it was Damascus.

That's the word, friend. Asa says, "Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me." He wants Ben-hadad to walk away from his deal with Baasha. It's like asking someone to ditch their other plans and come help you instead.

If Ben-hadad keeps his treaty with Baasha, nothing changes for Asa, and Baasha stays right at Ramah. That's why Asa asks the opposite. He says, "Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me." He needs that treaty broken.
Asa isn't asking for a bigger treaty with Baasha, baker. Asa wants the treaty with Baasha gone. He says, "Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me."

Yep, baker. When Baasha learned what had happened, "he stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work." The whole project just dropped. I think that's what a man does when he realizes the trouble has moved to his own cities.
Not finished, friend. The text says Baasha "stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work." The tools were put down, and the wall was left half done.
Nobody doubled anything, baker. Baasha stopped. The text says he "stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work" when he learned of it.

True, baker. The men of Judah "carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building." Then Asa used those materials to build up Geba and Mizpah. Baasha's own supplies got turned into Asa's building projects, and that's recycling at a royal level.

This one is true, friend. The text says Asa brought all the men of Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. Then with those materials Asa built up Geba and Mizpah. So Baasha's leftovers became Asa's walls.

explanations.answer: Asa relied on Aram and not the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the heart of it, baker. Hanani says, "Because you have relied on the king of Aram and not on the LORD your God…" The problem wasn't a lack of silver or a lack of armies. It was where Asa put his trust.

explanations.answer: Asa bowed down to the gods of Aram
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about Asa bowing to any gods of Aram, friend. Hanani's complaint is that Asa "relied on the king of Aram and not on the LORD your God." So the trouble was where Asa leaned for help.

explanations.answer: Asa made the deal on the Sabbath day
explanations.explanation: No Sabbath in this passage, baker. Hanani says, "Because you have relied on the king of Aram and not on the LORD your God…" The day on the calendar never comes up. The problem was who Asa leaned on.

True, baker. Hanani asks, "Were not the Cushites and Libyans a vast army with many chariots and horsemen?" Then he says, "Yet because you relied on the LORD, He delivered them into your hand." Hanani is pointing back to a time when Asa leaned on the LORD, and it went very differently.

This one is true, friend. Hanani says the Cushites and Libyans were a vast army with many chariots and horsemen. Then he says, "Yet because you relied on the LORD, He delivered them into your hand." He's reminding Asa how it went when he trusted the LORD.

explanations.answer: To show Himself strong for devoted hearts
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Hanani says, "For the eyes of the LORD roam to and fro over all the earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him." I love that line. The LORD is looking over all the earth for people who are fully His.

explanations.answer: To keep count of every army on earth
explanations.explanation: Hanani never mentions counting armies, baker. He says the eyes of the LORD roam "to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him." So the point is about devoted hearts, not army numbers.

explanations.answer: To find the kings who break treaties
explanations.explanation: Treaties come up earlier in the story, but not in this line. Hanani says the eyes of the LORD roam over all the earth "to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him." So the reason is about devoted hearts, baker.

That's right, friend. Hanani tells Asa, "You have acted foolishly in this matter. From now on, therefore, you will be at war." Asa bought a fix for one fight and got a whole season of fights. That's one expensive deal.
I wish it were that sweet, baker, but it's the opposite. Hanani says, "You have acted foolishly in this matter. From now on, therefore, you will be at war." The treasure didn't buy him peace.
Exile isn't what Hanani says, friend. He tells Asa, "You have acted foolishly in this matter. From now on, therefore, you will be at war." The word is war.

That's right, baker. The text says Asa was angry and "became so enraged over this matter that he put the man in prison." Hanani told him the truth, and Asa locked him up for it. I think that one hurts.
The text doesn't say Asa sent Hanani out of Judah, friend. It says Asa became so enraged that he put the man in prison. Hanani went from the king's presence to a cell.
No land is mentioned here, baker. The text says Asa "put the man in prison." That's what the enraged king did to Hanani.
Not quite, friend. Verse 10 says Asa put Hanani in prison, and then it adds, "And at the same time Asa oppressed some of the people." So Hanani wasn't the only one. This is a heavy part of the story.
You got it, baker. Asa put Hanani in prison, and "at the same time Asa oppressed some of the people." So the anger didn't stop at the seer. It's a heavy part of the story, and I won't joke about it.

That's what the text says, friend. In his illness Asa "did not seek the LORD, but only the physicians." The problem wasn't the doctors. It was that the LORD never got a call. I think Asa had a habit of looking everywhere else first.
Priests aren't mentioned here, baker. The text says that even in his illness Asa "did not seek the LORD, but only the physicians." So the ones he went to were the physicians.

No prophets in this part, friend. The text says Asa "did not seek the LORD, but only the physicians." Hanani the seer had already spoken to him earlier in the chapter, and this verse tells us who Asa turned to instead.

explanations.answer: In a tomb he cut out for himself
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says Asa "was buried in the tomb that he had cut out for himself in the City of David." He picked out his own resting place ahead of time. That's some serious planning.
Machpelah is a real cave, but it isn't Asa's. Abraham buried his wife Sarah there (Genesis 23:19). Asa was buried in the tomb he had cut out for himself in the City of David.

explanations.answer: In the garden of his own house
explanations.explanation: No garden burial in this story, friend. The text says Asa was buried in the tomb he had cut out for himself in the City of David. It was a tomb he had made himself, not a garden.
